newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan Sunni leader among 15 killed by bomb.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan Sunni leader among 15 killed by bomb.

text.p: A bomb exploded outside a courthouse in the Pakistani city of Lahore on Saturday, killing at least 15 people, including the leader of a militant Sunni Moslem group, and wounding 90, officials said.

The bomb, apparently left on a motorcycle, went off at about 12.30 p.m. (0730 GMT) as Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) group leader Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi and his deputy, Azam Tariq, arrived at the court to be greeted by supporters showering them with flowers.

Faruqi, SSP Patron-in-Chief, died in hospital while Tariq, who had survived a grenade and rocket attack in 1994 in the central province of Punjab, of which Lahore is the capital, was seriously wounded, doctors said.
One of Tariq's legs was shattered by the remote-controlled bomb, the official APP news agency said.
Eyewitnesses said most of the casualties were policemen, journalists, lawyers or SSP supporters. A big area outside the court was littered with limbs of the victims and police caps.
Doctors had earlier put the death toll at 12, but a senior local government official, Deputy Commissioner Kamran Lashari, said 15 people had died with 90 wounded.

Nobody claimed responsibility for the bombing, which appeared to be the latest move in a long-running feud between militant groups of the majority Sunni and minority Shi'ite Moslem sects that cost nearly 170 lives last year in Pakistan.
But APP quoted a police official as saying a man suspected of "some link with this act of sabotage" had been arrested while he trying to flee from the blast scene.
Faruqi and Tariq were due to appear before the Sessions Court in central Lahore on charges of involvement in sectarian killings of Shi'ites.
Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's predominantly Sunni population of over 130 million but are the majority in neighbouring Iran.

The secretary of Iran's National Security Council, Hassan Rowhani, urged the Pakistani government on Thursday to mount a "crackdown on terrorist groups in Pakistan and (prevent) the assassination of Shi'ite Moslems".
"The groups not only endanger Pakistan's security but also hamper the unity of Moslems," Rowhani, a Shi'ite cleric, told visiting Pakistani Foreign Minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan.
The SSP issued a statement on Friday calling the Iranian statement an interference in Pakistan's internal affairs.
Shi'ite militancy in Pakistan was fuelled by the 1979 Islamic revolution in Iran, sparking a fierce backlash from well-armed Sunni groups such as the SSP.
Two Shi'ite leaders were killed in separate incidents in Pakistan on December 31 and a Shi'ite activist was shot dead on Monday.

Sunni-Shi'ite disputes over Islamic beliefs have often spilled into violence in Pakistan. There has been a wave of such incidents in recent months in Punjab and North West Frontier province in which many scpores of people have died.
